title: Immersive Post-Realism/Reconstructionism - trying to identify a stylistic phenomenon in cinema.

commenti.body:
I’ve noticed in recent years a degree of resurgence of the modernist approach to storytelling in film & tv that I think overlaps with what you’re talking about. It’s a reembracing of earnestness that really stands out against the quintessential irony of postmodern storytelling. Sincerity instead of self awareness/meta. It also makes prominent use of symbols in a way that postmodernism had quite done away with and I think denigrated to audiences. A great example is Rings of Power, where the characters don’t act like “real” people even though what we’re seeing on screen is hyperreal, and the narrative is primarily about expressing theme (supported by motifs and other aspects of the language of the medium), like right at the forefront, rather than theme taking a narrative backseat to the postmodern rollercoaster of trope/subversion of trope followed by trope/subversion of trope. Audiences have rejected this as “bad writing” (not to say the writing is flawless I’m just zeroing in on this aspect) because that’s how postmodern storytelling has trained them, when it’s actually truer to Tolkiens modernist storytelling than Jackson’s action movie trilogy.

I think each film has its own context and its own appropriate way to tell its story, ie there is no one size fits all or one superior approach. I do think more variety is good though especially during this increasingly hyperconglomerized and hypercorporatized era of cinema. I would say fantasy with its roots in fairy tale specifically and folk tale generally is particularly well suited to this approach. A good example of a more warmly received text is Del Toros Pans Labyrinth. A really fun comparison is the more modernist Willy Wonka (1971) vs the more postmodern Charlie (2005).

Writing this in bed so probably not communicating my thoughts the best particularly with how it connects to what you’re talking about, but let me know your thoughts and I’d be stoked to have a discussion in this area about it.

Very interesting, I think I might've missed a bigger picture here and focused on a small element of a larger trend. I don't really watch a lot of new mainstream cinema because, as you pointed out, it's hypercorporatized. The films in question kinda stand out precisely because they seem to constitute a unique creative niche that does still express an authorial voice within the mostly voiceless/consumerist mainstream.

>I think each film has its own context and its own appropriate way to tell its story, ie there is no one size fits all or one superior approach.

Fully agree there. And Pan's Labyrinth is an excellent example of a fairy tale made in this style, I'll need to rewatch it someday (only seen it once, years ago).

I wouldn't really include Willy Wonka on my list, not that you didn't identify its contextual nature correctly (in the sense of the larger trend that I mentioned earlier in this comment), but I just find the story so intentionally surreal, any notion of realism is out of question. But I do see what you mean and agree with your overall point.

I haven't seen Rings of Power yet, though I'm planning to. Your comment made me wanna see it more.

Anyway, thanks for contributing to the discussion. Didn't think my post would resonate with anyone.

have you watched this video essay by the great Thomas Flight on what he calls "metamodernism" in films? It might be helpful to discern that vague feeling of yours: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5xEi8qg266g

It's interesting that you suggest this as a "stylistic phenomenon" which I would say is a better term than genre or sub-genre. I'm not completely convinced that it is a thing belonging to a particular time as you believe, or characteristic of a post-realist aesthetic movement or tendency, but rather a choice to blur the distinctions between realism and fantasy that can happen in any age. The very genre/tendency/whatever of "magical realism" which arguably goes back to Kafka or Borges speaks to the possibility of doing such a thing.

Do you know for example Vampyr by Dreyer from 1930? It's a vampire film but very grounded in realism. Very little happens that is supernatural, perhaps even nothing. So it falls between realism and genre fantasy, much like a lot of those you discuss. Black Narcissus by Powell/Pressburger (1947) is a similar example, I think. 

So what I'm really suggesting is that this tendency which you see goes back a long way into the history of cinema, and isn't really anything like a generic thing or a movement but rather an artistic preference that any filmmaker might choose. I think you could find examples of that from almost any year if you look for it.

To put it another way, I think your selection shows a little recency bias and a similar list of the "feel" of movies could go way back.
I haven't, but will tomorrow, thanks!

I think I might've not conveyed my point very well, but it's definitely not as simple as just an artistic preference. One of the things I outline in my Letterboxd list is that these are genre movies, because art movies (as I believe Vampyr is) are deconstructionist by nature. That's also true about Kafka, his books were definitely subversions of the traditional narratives of the time. Also, the word "fantasy" here isn't necessarily used to refer to magical creatures and stuff. It can be a fantasy, as in an idealization. If you look at the list, most movies there don't have really fantastical elements, but despite their attempt at realism, still end up feeling like they're embracing a kind of idealized reality that had been deconstructed. With every movie on the list, it's a kind of return to old tropes, but with a new realistic flavour.

OK, I'll have to consider your descriptions more closely before I get back to you again. I'd hate to blunder in without considering it more. 

What I'm working on right now is a different thing but maybe runs parallel to your identification of trends in genre movies. I'm thinking a lot about "ironic meta" in recent film output and when it goes well and when it fails. This is obviously not the same thing as what you're talking about, but there is maybe a related strand to do with sincerity vs irony. 

At present my own ideas on that are even less defined than yours but there's a small chance the strands might connect in some way.

I would be better able to understand what you're trying to say if you were to actually explain how an example or two (or three) express it. I'm looking at the list and not fully getting it just from that.

I feel like what you're working on is almost the opposite of mine, but it might connect, as you say, in the sense that it's probably on the same spectrum, just the opposite end. Either way, would love to see it.
Click the "read notes" button. There are explanations under every film.
Extremely astute comment re:Rings of Power.

Very interesting and well-made video. I feel like the movies in my list probably fall under the general cinematic zeitgeist shift that is exemplified in meta-modernism, but they engage more with it stylistically rather than thematically or structurally. I mean there is some thematic engagement, but it's more like a stylistic solution to a thematic question, so it still ends up being a stylistic trend more than anything, although perhaps you could call it a sub-trend that exists within the larger meta-modernist trend. Then again, it might only be adjacently meta-modernist, since it doesn't exactly provide meta-modernist subtext (like the movies analyzed in the video), but rather we derive meta-modernist context from analyzing the place of these films among their contemporaries. Or to describe it in less-confusing language, some of them are very simple films that don't really possess much of inherent meaning, while those that do possess it don't necessarily express the ideas identified in this video as meta-modern.

But I'm not sure about anything. Definitely a lot of food for thought. Thanks for sending the video.

Interesting! When reading your description, The Dark Knight immediately sprung to mind, and I see that you have the whole trilogy on your list.

Some other movies to consider: Tenet, Joker, Godzilla (2014). Perhaps Blade Runner 2049? Casino Royale (2006)?

I think Zack Snyder *thinks* he’s doing what you’re describing.

Thank you! If you thought about The Dark Knight, you probably understood exactly what I meant right away.

I haven't seen Tenet, Blade Runner 2049 or Casino Royale yet, but Godzilla (2014) is a great suggestion! I probably need a rewatch before adding it though because I haven't seen it in almost a decade now.

I want to avoid adding stuff like Joker though, because it seems to be existing in that superhero bubble that formed particularly after The Avengers. And its stylistic choices don't deviate much from what had already been the status quo (thanks partially to Nolan's take). In other words, it only stands out as a serious and realistic work if you expect it not to be, but in 2019 was anybody expecting anything else though? I know I wasn't. If anything, I find Joker's depiction in Suicide Squad (2016) more befitting the list, because it combines elements of the deconstructed Joker from the Nolan movies and its less-realistic comic book inspiration. But Suicide Squad (2016) is too silly of a movie to make this list. On this note though, the last Batman movie might actually make this list, but I gotta rewatch it to crystalize my thoughts.

>I think Zack Snyder thinks he’s doing what you’re describing.

Haha, I dunno what he thinks, but he's too much of an edgelord to fit this category. His movies can only be one thing, regardless of what the source material was. Plus they all convey suspiciously right-wing/objectivist narratives. I prefer to stay far away from that guy.
